newsitem.title: FINLAND: Bethlehem says steel a bargain, demand solid.
newsitem.headline: Bethlehem says steel a bargain, demand solid.

text.p: Steel can be had for bargain prices and demand for steel among key users in the United States is solid, Bethlehem Steel chairman and CEO Curtis Barnette said on Monday.
Steel prices were still below 1995 levels, but on the mend, Barnette told a Reuters reporter at the first day of the annual congress of the International Iron and Steel Institute (IISI) here.
"There has been an improvement (in steel prices), but 1996 pricing is not yet back to the 1995 level," he said.
"Steel is a bargain in terms of affordability" Barnette added.
Demand for steel was solid among key users.
"The automobile sector is very good, construction is good, machinery and equipment is good," he said, referring to U.S. markets.

Bethlehem Steel is expecting "conservative but steady" U.S. gross domestic product growth at a pace of 2.2-2.5 percent throughout 1996 and into 1997, he said, adding inflation appeared to be "well under control".
"1997 will look a lot like 1996 in terms of general economic conditions," Barnette said.
In the United States, "domestic steel industry shipments will be at the 97-98 million tonne level" in 1996, he said. In 1995, U.S. steel production totalled 93.5 million tonnes.

A rise in steel prices is seen starting in the United States. Asked whether U.S. producers would be vulnerable to competition from lower-price imports if domestic steel prices took off, Barnette said:
"If imports are traded fairly in the U.S. and on the world market, U.S. steel producers will compete effectively against imports."
